gloss_terse: to test thoroughly, put to the proof; to tempt or try God by demanding signs or proofs of his power
gloss_readable: An intensified form of πειράζω (the ἐκ- prefix adding force), this verb describes the act of putting someone—especially God—to the test. In the Synoptic temptation narratives (Matt 4:7; Luke 4:12), Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:16 against Satan: 'You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.' Paul warns the Corinthians against repeating Israel's wilderness provocations (1 Cor 10:9). The lawyer in Luke 10:25 tests Jesus with a question, though the word carries a lighter nuance there.

senses.1: To put to the test in a presumptuous or provocative manner, especially testing God by demanding proof of his faithfulness or power. All four NT occurrences cluster around this meaning. Spanish 'tentar' and French 'tenter' preserve the Latin temptare root; English translations split between 'test' (for human agents) and 'tempt' (when directed at God). Matt 4:7 and Luke 4:12 cite the LXX Deuteronomy prohibition; 1 Cor 10:9 recalls Israel's wilderness provocations; Luke 10:25 softens to a testing inquiry.

gloss_terse: to uproot, pull out by the roots; to eradicate completely
gloss_readable: Drawn from agricultural language, this verb describes the violent act of tearing a plant out by its roots. Jesus uses it in the parable of the wheat and tares, warning against premature uprooting that would harm good plants (Matt 13:29), and declares that every plant not planted by the Father will be uprooted (Matt 15:13). In Luke 17:6, even a mulberry tree obeys the command to uproot itself. Jude 1:12 applies the image metaphorically to false teachers—'uprooted, twice dead.'

senses.1: To pull up by the roots, to eradicate or destroy completely. The agricultural metaphor carries theological weight across all four occurrences. Spanish 'desarraigar' and French 'déraciner' both transparently reflect the root-removal imagery (raíz, racine). In Matt 13:29 the concern is collateral damage from premature uprooting; Matt 15:13 announces divine judgment; Luke 17:6 illustrates faith's power over nature; Jude 1:12 extends the metaphor to spiritual barrenness.

gloss_terse: to set forth, explain in detail; to expose (a child); to lay out publicly
gloss_readable: This compound verb (ἐκ + τίθημι, 'to place out') carries two distinct senses in Acts. In Acts 7:21 it refers to the exposure of the infant Moses—the ancient practice of abandoning unwanted newborns. In Acts 11:4, 18:26, and 28:23, it means to set forth or explain something in orderly detail. Spanish captures both registers: 'exponer' covers physical exposure and intellectual exposition alike. The shift from literal placement to rhetorical presentation follows a natural semantic path.

senses.1: To expose a newborn child by placing it outside, abandoning it to the elements. This technical sense appears in Acts 7:21, where Moses is described as having been 'exposed' (ἐκτεθέντος). Spanish 'habiendo-sido-expuesto' and French 'exposer' use cognate forms preserving the physical imagery of setting out. The passive participle emphasizes the infant's vulnerability and the providential rescue that follows.

gloss_terse: to shake off or shake out, as dust from feet or garments, signaling rejection or disassociation
gloss_readable: A vivid gestural verb describing the forceful shaking off of dust or debris. In the Gospels, Jesus instructs his disciples to shake the dust from their feet when leaving an unreceptive town—a prophetic sign of judgment (Matt 10:14; Mark 6:11). Paul and Barnabas perform this same gesture against hostile opponents in Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51). In Acts 18:6, Paul shakes out his garments against the Corinthian synagogue, echoing Nehemiah 5:13. Every NT use carries symbolic force beyond the physical act.

senses.1: To shake off or shake out as a symbolic act of protest, renunciation, or transferred responsibility. All four NT occurrences function as prophetic gestures rather than mere hygiene. Spanish 'sacudir' and French 'secouer' convey the vigorous physical motion. Matt 10:14 and Mark 6:11 describe dust shaken from feet as testimony against rejecting towns; Acts 13:51 repeats the gesture against persecutors; Acts 18:6 intensifies to shaking out garments, recalling Nehemiah's oath-gesture.

gloss_terse: smaller, lesser, inferior; younger or lower in status or degree
gloss_readable: The comparative form of μικρός (by way of ἐλαχύς), this adjective conveys 'less' across multiple dimensions—size, age, rank, or quality. At the wedding in Cana, the steward notes that the inferior wine normally comes last (John 2:10). Paul quotes the oracle about Jacob and Esau: 'the elder shall serve the younger' (Rom 9:12). The 'undeniably lesser is blessed by the greater' principle governs the Melchizedek argument in Hebrews 7:7. French 'moindre' and 'plus petit' helpfully distinguish degree from size.

senses.1: Smaller, lesser, or inferior in degree, rank, age, or quality. This comparative adjective flexes across contexts: John 2:10 contrasts wine quality (lesser vs. good); Rom 9:12 distinguishes the younger/lesser son in the Jacob-Esau narrative; 1 Tim 5:9 sets a minimum age threshold (not less than sixty); Heb 7:7 establishes a hierarchical principle where the lesser receives blessing from the greater. Spanish uses 'menor' (younger/lesser) and 'inferior,' reflecting the dual age-rank semantic range.

gloss_terse: to remain in, abide by, persevere in; to continue steadfast in a commitment or place
gloss_readable: A compound of ἐν + μένω, this verb intensifies the idea of remaining by emphasizing the 'in-ness'—staying within a commitment, a place, or a covenant. Paul and Barnabas exhort new believers to continue in the faith (Acts 14:22), while Paul himself remained two full years in Rome (Acts 28:30). The covenantal sense is sharpest in Hebrews 8:9 and Galatians 3:10, where failure to abide in God's covenant or law brings consequences. Spanish 'permanecer' and French 'demeurer' both stress durational persistence.

senses.1: To remain steadfast in, to abide by or persevere within a commitment, place, or covenant. The ἐν- prefix localizes the remaining: one stays within the faith (Acts 14:22), within a dwelling (Acts 28:30), or within the terms of a covenant (Heb 8:9, quoting Jer 31:32). Gal 3:10 warns about remaining within everything written in the law. Spanish 'permanecer' and French 'demeurer/persévérance' capture both the spatial and the moral-commitment dimensions of this verb.

gloss_terse: demonstration, proof, evidence; a visible display that establishes something as true
gloss_readable: This noun denotes a concrete showing-forth that makes something evident or provable. Paul uses it twice in Romans 3:25-26 to describe Christ's sacrificial death as God's 'demonstration' of his righteousness—not merely a claim but a public exhibit of justice. In 2 Corinthians 8:24, the Corinthians are urged to show proof of their love before the churches. Philippians 1:28 speaks of the opponents' resistance as evidence of their destruction. Each use demands that the proof be visible to others.

senses.1: A public demonstration or visible proof that establishes a truth-claim before witnesses. All four NT uses emphasize externally verifiable evidence. In Rom 3:25-26, God sets forth Christ as a demonstration (ἔνδειξιν) of divine righteousness—twice repeated for emphasis. In 2 Cor 8:24, the Corinthians must display proof (ἔνδειξιν) of their love. Phil 1:28 treats the opponents' boldness as evidence (ἔνδειξις) of coming judgment. French 'démonstration' and German 'Beweis' both capture the forensic, evidentiary quality.

gloss_terse: glorious, splendid, honored; held in high esteem or notable in appearance
gloss_readable: Derived from δόξα ('glory'), this adjective describes persons or things that possess or reflect honor, splendor, or distinction. In Luke 7:25, it characterizes the fine clothing of those in royal courts. Luke 13:17 reports that the crowd rejoiced at all the 'glorious things' Jesus was doing. Paul uses it ironically in 1 Corinthians 4:10—'you are honored, we are dishonored.' Ephesians 5:27 presents the church as Christ's bride: 'glorious, without spot or wrinkle.'

senses.1: Glorious, splendid, or held in high honor—describing persons of distinction or things of notable quality. The root in δόξα ('glory, reputation') grounds every use. Luke 7:25 applies it to splendid garments; Luke 13:17 to Jesus' remarkable deeds; Eph 5:27 to the church's eschatological perfection. Paul's use in 1 Cor 4:10 is bitterly ironic: 'you are ἔνδοξοι, but we are dishonored.' Spanish 'gloriosa/honrados' and French 'glorieux/magnifique' split the honor-splendor range helpfully.

gloss_terse: thought, reflection, inner deliberation; the content or process of pondering within the mind
gloss_readable: From ἐν + θυμός ('in the spirit/mind'), this noun denotes the inner workings of thought—what one turns over in the heart. Jesus perceives the ἐνθυμήσεις of the scribes in Matthew 9:4 and of the Pharisees in Matthew 12:25, exposing hidden hostile reasoning. Acts 17:29 uses it for the products of human artistic imagination. Hebrews 4:12 declares the word of God a discerner of the 'thoughts and intentions of the heart,' pairing ἐνθυμήσεων with ἐννοιῶν.

senses.1: Inner thoughts, reflections, or deliberations—especially those concealed from others but transparent to God. The ἐν-θυμ- root ('within the spirit') points to the interior quality of these cogitations. In Matt 9:4 and 12:25, Jesus supernaturally perceives the hostile ἐνθυμήσεις of religious opponents. Acts 17:29 extends to human artistic conceptions (the 'imaginings' behind idol-craft). Heb 4:12 pairs it with ἐννοιῶν ('intentions'), underscoring the penetrating reach of God's word. Spanish 'pensamientos' and French 'pensée' straightforwardly render 'thoughts.'

gloss_readable: The indeclinable Greek numeral for ninety, appearing exclusively in the parables of the lost sheep. In both Matthew 18:12-13 and Luke 15:4-7, the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine in safety to search for the one that has strayed. The number's sole narrative function in the NT is to dramatize the value God places on each individual—the ninety-nine safe sheep make the rescue of the one all the more striking.

senses.1: The cardinal number ninety, used in the NT only within the compound 'ninety-nine' in the parable of the lost sheep. All four occurrences (Matt 18:12-13; Luke 15:4, 7) present the ninety-nine as the flock left behind while the shepherd pursues the single lost one. Spanish 'noventa' and French 'quatre-vingt-dix' (literally 'four-twenty-ten') render the number straightforwardly, though the French vigesimal construction is a curiosity. The theological weight lies not in the number itself but in the contrast it creates.
